title: Modal Verbs

toc.title: 22.1 The nine modals and what each one means
22.4 Past and perfect forms — modal + have + V3
22.5 The mistakes Nepali speakers make most

html:
Modal verbs are the nine little helpers — can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must — that do not describe an action but comment on it: how possible it is, how necessary it is, how polite you are being. NEB Q7 sets them almost every year, usually as a gap to be filled with a suitable modal, or as a sentence to be corrected. Because each modal carries several meanings, the safe method is to read the whole sentence, name the meaning you need — ability, permission, obligation, deduction, advice — and only then pick the word.

The five grammatical rules that never change
  1. A modal takes no -s in the third person: He can swim, not ~~cans~~.
  2. A modal is followed by the bare infinitive (V1, no to): She must go, not ~~must to go~~. Only ought keeps to.
  3. Questions and negatives need no do: Can he drive? / He cannot drive.
  4. Two modals cannot stand together: ~~will can~~ → will be able to; ~~must have to~~ → must or have to, never both.
  5. Modals have no infinitive, no -ing and no participle; for the missing forms use a semi-modal: to be able to, having had to, will have to.

22.1 The nine modals and what each one means

Modal Meanings it carries Example Past / substitute form
can ability; permission (informal); general possibility; request She can speak Maithili. could; was/were able to; be allowed to
could past ability; polite request; present possibility; past permission Could you lend me your notes? could have + V3
may permission (formal); possibility (about 50 per cent); wish You may leave after the bell. might; was/were allowed to
might weaker possibility; very polite request; past of may in reporting It might rain this evening. might have + V3
will future; willingness; promise; strong prediction; characteristic habit I will carry your bag. would
would polite request/offer; past habit; unreal situations; past of will Would you like some tea? would have + V3
shall offers and suggestions with I / we; formal legal obligation Shall I open the window? should
should advice; expectation; obligation (weaker than must) You should see a doctor. should have + V3
must strong obligation; prohibition (mustn't); confident deduction He must be over sixty. had to (obligation); must have + V3 (deduction)

22.2 The meanings, one by one

Ability

Can for the present, could for general ability in the past, and be able to wherever a modal cannot go.

  • Bishal can solve any sum in his head.
  • At fourteen I could cycle from Butwal to Bhairahawa. (general past ability)
  • After three attempts the team was able to reach the summit. (one specific success — here could is wrong)
  • By next year she will be able to drive. (no two modals, so be able to)
Ability: the two errors that are everywhere

✗ He can able to speak Chinese. → ✓ He can speak Chinese. / ✓ He is able to speak Chinese. You may use one of them, never both. ✗ We could not able to finish the paper. → ✓ We could not finish the paper. / ✓ We were not able to finish the paper. ✗ I will can help you. → ✓ I will be able to help you.

Permission and prohibition

Function Words used Example
Asking permission Can I …? (informal), Could I …? (polite), May I …? (formal), Might I …? (very formal) May I come in, sir?
Giving permission can, may, be allowed to You may use the library after four.
Refusing permission cannot, may not You may not take the question paper out.
Prohibition (a rule, an order) must not Candidates mustn't carry mobile phones.
No obligation (free to choose) needn't, don't have to You needn't come on Saturday.
*Mustn't* and *needn't* are opposites, not twins

You mustn't park here = it is forbidden. You needn't park here = you are free not to; there is no need. Every year a candidate writes needn't where the sentence means "forbidden".

Obligation and necessity

  • must — the obligation comes from the speaker, or is felt inside: I must stop wasting time.
  • have to / has to — the obligation comes from outside: rules, the timetable, other people: We have to wear the college uniform.
  • had to — the past of both. Must has no past form: Yesterday I had to work late (never ~~I must worked~~).
  • should / ought to — a duty that is weaker than must: A citizen ought to pay tax.
  • be to — a formal instruction or arrangement: You are to report to the ward office at ten.

Advice and suggestion

Strength Form Example
gentle could, might You could try the evening class.
normal should, ought to You should revise the whole unit.
strong, about now had better (+ bare infinitive) You'd better leave now or you'll miss the bus.
suggestion, including the speaker shall we, let's, why don't we Shall we start?
preference would rather (+ bare infinitive) I'd rather walk than wait.

Had better is about one particular occasion and hints at a bad result if the advice is ignored; should is a general opinion. The negative is had better not: You'd better not tell him.

Possibility and deduction

This is where the exam separates candidates, so learn the scale.

  • must — the only possible explanation: The lights are off; they must have gone out.
  • can't / cannot — the impossible explanation. It is the negative of deductive must, not mustn't: He can't be in Jumla; I saw him in Kathmandu an hour ago.
  • may / might / could — one of several possibilities: She may be in the library. It might snow tonight.
  • can for general possibility (what sometimes happens): Jumla can be bitterly cold in Magh. Compare the particular possibility: It may be cold in Jumla tomorrow.

Habit, willingness and characteristic behaviour

  • used to + V1 — a past habit or state that has stopped: There used to be a wooden bridge here.
  • would + V1 — a repeated past action in a description (not for states): Every Dashain grandmother would make selroti for the whole village.
  • will for a present characteristic habit: He will sit reading for hours.
  • be used to + V-ing — accustomed to (a different structure altogether): She is used to walking three kilometres to school.

22.3 Semi-modals

Semi-modals supply the forms the nine modals lack, and add meanings of their own.

Semi-modal Meaning Example Note
have to / has to / had to external obligation I had to renew my licence. supplies the past and future of must
be able to ability He has been able to walk since March. supplies the missing forms of can
be allowed to permission We were allowed to leave early. past of permission can/may
ought to duty, expectation You ought to thank her. the only modal with to
had better urgent advice We'd better hurry. bare infinitive; negative had better not
would rather preference I'd rather not say. bare infinitive
used to discontinued past habit He used to smoke. question/negative with did: Did he use to smoke?
be supposed to what is expected or arranged You are supposed to wear a helmet. often implies it is not being done
need necessity You needn't shout. (modal) / You don't need to shout. (main verb) modal need has no -s and takes V1
dare courage He dare not complain. (modal) / He didn't dare to complain. (main verb) rare except in fixed phrases
be going to intention, prediction from evidence She is going to apply for the scholarship. not a modal, but tested with them

22.4 Past and perfect forms — modal + have + V3

A modal followed by have + past participle talks about the past. Each combination says something precise about whether the action actually happened.

Perfect modal Meaning Did it happen?
must have + V3 I am sure it happened yes
can't / couldn't have + V3 I am sure it did not happen no
may / might have + V3 possibly it happened unknown
could have + V3 it was possible, but it did not happen (or: unused ability) usually no
should / ought to have + V3 it was the right thing, and it was not done no — and that was a mistake
shouldn't have + V3 it was done, and it was wrong yes
needn't have + V3 it was done, but it was unnecessary yes
didn't need to + V1 it was unnecessary, so normally it was not done usually no
would have + V3 an unreal past result (see Unit 28) no

Compare the pair the board loves:

  • I needn't have taken an umbrella — it did not rain. (I took it; it was a waste)
  • I didn't need to take an umbrella, so I left it at home. (no need, so I did not take it)

22.5 The mistakes Nepali speakers make most

✗ Wrong ✓ Right Rule broken
I must have to go now. I must go now. / I have to go now. never two obligation words together
You should have to submit it today. You should submit it today. should is complete by itself
He can able to drive. He can drive. / He is able to drive. can + bare infinitive
She could not able to attend. She could not attend. / She was not able to attend. same rule in the negative
I will can meet you. I will be able to meet you. two modals are impossible
He cans play the madal. He can play the madal. a modal takes no -s
We should to respect our teachers. We should respect our teachers. no to after should
You had better to consult a doctor. You had better consult a doctor. had better + bare infinitive
Does he can swim? Can he swim? modals need no do
May be he is at home. Maybe he is at home. / He may be at home. maybe (one word) = perhaps
Yesterday I must submit the form. Yesterday I had to submit the form. must has no past
I am used to go there on foot. I used to go there on foot. / I am used to going there on foot. two different structures
Would you mind to open the door? Would you mind opening the door? mind + V-ing
He mustn't worry, there is no hurry. He needn't worry, there is no hurry. mustn't forbids; needn't releases
Worked item 22.1 — choosing between *could* and *was able to*

Problem. Fill in with the correct form: The house was burning fiercely, but the fire brigade ____ rescue everyone inside.

Solution — step by step.

  1. Name the meaning. This is about ability in the past.
  2. General ability or one particular success? The sentence describes one difficult occasion on which the rescue actually succeeded.
  3. Apply the rule. Could is used for a general past ability ("I could swim at five"). For a single achievement — managing to do something on one occasion — English uses was / were able to or managed to.
  4. Fit the subject. The fire brigade is singular → was.

Answer. … but the fire brigade was able to rescue everyone inside.

(In the negative, couldn't is perfectly correct even for a single occasion: They couldn't rescue the cat.)

Worked item 22.2 — a deduction about the past

Problem. Rewrite using a modal: I am sure Rita did not take my umbrella, because she left before the rain started.

Solution — step by step.

  1. Name the meaning. The speaker is sure about something in the past, and the certainty is negative.
  2. Choose the modal. Certainty that something is false is can't (or couldn't), never mustn't. Mustn't means "it is forbidden".
  3. Make it past. A modal is made past by adding have + past participle.

Answer. Rita can't have taken my umbrella; she left before the rain started.

The positive twin would be: Rita must have taken my umbrella.

Worked item 22.3 — correcting a sentence with several modal faults

Problem. Correct: Since I must have to reach the airport by six, I think I will can book a taxi, but you should to come with me, isn't it?

Solution — one fault at a time.

  1. must have to stacks two obligation forms. Keep one: have to (the deadline is external).
  2. will can stacks two modals. Replace the second with its semi-modal: will be able to — but here the plain future is simpler: I will book a taxi.
  3. should to come — should takes the bare infinitive: should come.
  4. The tag must match the statement. The main clause is you should come, so the tag is shouldn't you?

Answer. Since I have to reach the airport by six, I think I will book a taxi, but you should come with me, shouldn't you?**

Chapter summary

  • The nine modals are can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must; they take no -s, no do, and a bare infinitive.
  • Two modals never stand together: use a semi-modal (will be able to, have to).
  • Ability: can / could for general ability, was/were able to for a single past success, be able to for the missing forms.
  • Permission: can < could < may < might in formality. Prohibition is mustn't; absence of obligation is needn't / don't have to.
  • Obligation: must (from the speaker) vs have to (from outside); the past of both is had to.
  • Advice: should / ought to, and had better + bare infinitive for urgent advice on one occasion.
  • Certainty scale: must (sure it is true) > will / should > may > might / could > can't (sure it is false).
  • Past habit: used to + V1 (habits and states), would + V1 (repeated actions only); be used to + V-ing means "accustomed to".
  • Perfect modals: must have (it happened), can't have (it did not), may/might have (unknown), should have (it did not, and should have), needn't have (it did, unnecessarily).

Practice questions

Fill in the blanks with a suitable modal or semi-modal (1 mark each)

  1. She ____ speak three languages fluently. [1]
  2. ____ I use your pen for a moment, sir? [1]
  3. Students ____ not use mobile phones in the examination hall. [1]
  4. You ____ hurry; there is still half an hour left. [1]
  5. The lights are on, so somebody ____ be inside. [1]
  6. He ____ be in Pokhara — I met him in Bhaktapur this morning. [1]
  7. Yesterday I ____ stay late at the office to finish the report. [1]
  8. There ____ to be a big pipal tree at this corner, but it was cut down. [1]
  9. You ____ better see a doctor before the swelling gets worse. [1]
  10. After two hours of digging, the rescuers ____ to reach the trapped miners. [1]
Answers

1. can — present ability.

2. May (or Could) — asking formal permission.

3. must — must not states a prohibition.

4. needn't — there is no necessity; mustn't would wrongly forbid hurrying.

5. must — the only likely explanation, so a confident deduction.

6. can't — certainty that something is false is can't, not mustn't.

7. had to — must has no past form.

8. used — used to be is a discontinued past state.

9. had — had better + bare infinitive gives urgent advice.

10. were able — one particular success in the past, so were able to.

Correct the errors in the following sentences (1 mark each)

  1. I must have to submit the assignment before Friday. [1]
  2. My younger brother can able to recite the whole poem. [1]
  3. She cans drive a scooter. [1]
  4. We should to help the flood victims. [1]
  5. Does he can come with us tomorrow? [1]
  6. He had better to apologise to his teacher. [1]
  7. I will can finish the work by evening. [1]
  8. They could not able to solve the last question. [1]
  9. I am used to go to school on foot when I was a child. [1]
  10. You mustn't buy a ticket; entry is free today. [1]
Answers

11. I have to (or must) submit the assignment before Friday. — one obligation word only.

12. My younger brother can recite (or is able to recite) the whole poem.

13. She can drive a scooter. — a modal never takes -s.

14. We should help the flood victims. — no to after should.

15. Can he come with us tomorrow? — modals form questions without do.

16. He had better apologise to his teacher. — bare infinitive after had better.

17. I will be able to finish the work by evening. — two modals cannot stand together.

18. They could not solve (or were not able to solve) the last question.

19. I used to go to school on foot when I was a child. — a discontinued past habit.

20. You needn't buy a ticket; entry is free today. — no necessity, not prohibition.

Rewrite as instructed (1 mark each)

  1. It is not necessary for you to attend the rehearsal. — Rewrite using needn't. [1]
  2. I am sure he has forgotten the meeting. — Rewrite using a perfect modal. [1]
  3. It was wrong of you to shout at the conductor. — Rewrite using shouldn't. [1]
  4. Perhaps she missed the last bus. — Rewrite using might. [1]
  5. It is forbidden to pluck flowers in this garden. — Rewrite using mustn't. [1]
  6. I took a raincoat, but there was no rain at all. — Rewrite using needn't have. [1]
Answers

21. You needn't attend the rehearsal. — needn't + bare infinitive shows absence of necessity.

22. He must have forgotten the meeting. — certainty about the past is must have + V3.

23. You shouldn't have shouted at the conductor. — the act was done and it was wrong.

24. She might have missed the last bus. — a past possibility.

25. You mustn't pluck flowers in this garden. — mustn't states a prohibition.

26. I needn't have taken a raincoat. — the action was done, but it turned out to be unnecessary.
